chunks: TTL vs CMOS logic families. The question: TTL vs CMOS?
TTL and CMOS are two families of digital logic chips. TTL is built from bipolar transistors and draws current all the time.
CMOS is built from paired MOSFETs and draws almost nothing when idle. Their voltage thresholds for "high" and "low" differ, so connecting them needs care.
Imagine two languages that use the same words but draw the line between "loud" and "quiet" at different volumes.
A listener from one may miss the other's "loud" if it stops just short of their line. That is what can happen at a TTL-to-CMOS connection.
The fix is a translator, a chip designed to accept one language and speak the other.
Q1 is the input transistor (its emitter is the input; NAND gates use a multi-emitter Q1).
Q2 is a phase splitter that drives the totem pole: Q3 + diode pull the output up, Q4 pulls it down. The diode makes sure Q3 is off when Q4 is on.
Every DC path here draws current, which is where TTL's static power comes from.
TTL: transistor-transistor logic, a bipolar family such as 74LS. CMOS: logic built from complementary MOSFETs.
Input thresholds: the lowest voltage an input is sure to read as "high", and the highest it is sure to read as "low". In between, the reading is not guaranteed.
Noise margin: the gap between what an output guarantees and what an input needs. 74HCT: CMOS with TTL-compatible input thresholds.
A 5 volts TTL output only guarantees at least 2. 4 volts for a high. A 74HC input on 5 volts needs about 3.
5 volts, which is 70% of its supply, before it is sure to read a high (datasheets often quote 3. 15 volts, measured at a 4. 5 volts supply).
So the TTL signal might not be read as high at all. A 74HCT input accepts anything above about 2. 0 volts as high, so it works.
The usual choice today is CMOS, since it is faster and uses less power. That is the whole idea.
"TTL is bipolar logic: multi-emitter BJT inputs and a totem-pole NPN output, 5 volts only. CMOS uses complementary MOSFETs.
TTL draws static current, a few mW per gate, and its inputs source current; CMOS draws almost nothing static and its inputs are high impedance but must not float.
TTL thresholds are fixed at 0. 8 and 2. 0 volts with outputs guaranteed only to 2. 4 volts, while CMOS swings rail to rail with thresholds that scale with V DD .
So a TTL output can't reliably drive a 5 volts HC input, which is what HCT parts fix."
